# Faceting {#ggplot2-facets}

## Introduction

:::{.callout-note}
## Why this chart

Facets split one plot into small multiples sharing scales, so group differences are comparable.
:::

:::{.callout-warning}
## Common pitfall

Too many facet levels shrink each panel past readability; filter or wrap sensibly.
:::

In this chapter, we will learn about faceting, i.e. splitting one plot into
panels, one per group.

```{r facet, echo=FALSE, eval=TRUE, results='hide', message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(readr)
```

Let us continue with the scatter plot examining the relationship between 
displacement and miles per gallon, but let us make one additional change.
We now want 3 sub plots, one for each type of cylinder. How can we do this? We can
split or group the data by cylinder type and plot the subset of data, which
means dealing with 3 different data sets, plotting 3 plots and arranging them
for comparison. ggplot2 offers the following 2 functions, which allow us to plot
subsets of data with a simple formula-based interface:

- `facet_grid()`
- `facet_wrap()`

Faceting allows us to create multiple sub plots. It partitions a plot into a 
matrix of panels, with each panel showing a different subset of data.

## Arrange facets in a grid {#facet-grid}

### Stack facets vertically {#facet-grid-vertical}

`facet_grid()` allows us to split up the data by one or two discrete variables 
and create sub plots. The sub plots can be arranged horizontally or vertically 
using a formula of the form `vertical ~ horizontal`. In the example below, 3 
sub plots are created, one for each level of the `cyl` variable, and 
the sub plots are arranged vertically.


```{r facet2, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) + 
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(cyl ~ .)
```

### Arrange facets horizontally {#facet-grid-horizontal}

Below we reproduce the previous example but arrange the sub plots horizontally.

```{r facet1, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) + 
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(. ~ cyl)
```

### Facet rows and columns together {#facet-grid-rows-columns}

Sometimes, we might want different discrete variables to represent the
horizontal and vertical direction. In the example below, we examine the 
relationship between displacement and miles per gallon for different combinations
of the `cyl` and `gear` variables. 

```{r facet3, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) + 
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(cyl ~ gear)
```

Below, we switch the variables representing the vertical and horizontal 
directions.

```{r facet4, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) + 
  geom_point() +
  facet_grid(gear ~ cyl)
```

### Use free scales in a facet grid {#facet-grid-free-scales}

If you observe the second example carefully, the range of the `X` axis is the
same for all the 3 sub plots, i.e. it is a fixed range. You can allow each of the sub 
plots to have a different range using the `scales` argument and supplying it the
value `'free'`. 

```{r facet5, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg, color = factor(cyl))) +
  geom_point() + 
  facet_grid(. ~ cyl, scales = "free")
```

Now, each of the sub plots has a different range.

### Move facet labels with switch {#facet-grid-switch}

In the third example, the labels are displayed at the top for `X` axis and 
at the right for the `Y` axis. You can change this using the `switch` argument 
and supplying the value `'both'`. The labels will now be displayed at the bottom 
for the `X` axis and at the left for the `Y` axis. If you just want to change the 
labels for a particular axis, use the values `x` and `y` for the `X` and `Y`
axes respectively.

```{r facet6, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  facet_grid(cyl ~ gear, switch = "both") 
```

## Wrap facets into panels {#facet-wrap}

`facet_wrap()` allows us to arrange sub plots in a certain number of rows and 
columns. In the example below, we will use `facet_wrap()` to arrange the sub 
plots in a single row.

```{r facet7, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cyl)
```

### Set facet rows {#facet-wrap-rows}

To arrange the sub plots in a specific number of rows, use the `nrow` argument.
In the example below, we arrange the sub plots in 2 rows.

```{r facet8, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cyl, nrow = 2)
```

### Set facet columns {#facet-wrap-columns}

Here, we arrange the sub plots in 3 columns instead of rows using the `ncol`
argument.

```{r facet9, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cyl, ncol = 3)
```

### Use free scales in wrapped facets {#facet-wrap-free-scales}

You can allow each of the sub plots to have a different range using the `scales` 
argument and supplying it the value `'free'`. 

```{r facet12, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cyl, scales = "free")
```

### Set facet rows and columns {#facet-wrap-rows-columns}

If 2 discrete variables are used to create the sub plots, we can either use
the formula interface to specify the variables:

```{r facet10, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~cyl + gear, nrow = 2)
```

or use a character vector of variable names.

```{r facet11, fig.align='center'}
ggplot(mtcars, aes(disp, mpg)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(c("cyl", "gear"), ncol = 2)
```

## Exercises

1. Facet `disp` vs `mpg` by cylinders with `facet_wrap()`.
2. Grid `gear` rows against `carb` columns with `facet_grid()`.
3. Decide when facets beat color grouping and justify it.
